clue.text: Visit prison, you say? It's worth viewing

indicators.note: the speaker's 'you say' tells us to judge the phrase by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: to visit someone is to see them; NICK is British slang for a prison or police station

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a trip to a jail is a worthwhile outing.
explanation.walkthrough: NICK is everyday British slang for a prison or police station. Spoken together, SEE NICK matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A view or place that is pleasing to look at is described as picturesque, worth a look.

clue.text: Shop repairing chairs, note

indicators.note: repairing suggests fixing things by putting them back together differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A furniture shop fixes chairs and leaves a note.
explanation.definitionFit: A retail outlet belonging to a multiple-branch company is a kind of shop.

clue.text: One judo expert standing up on river bottom

indicators.note: in a down entry, standing up means the letters read upwards, so in reverse order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
a DAN is a grade of black belt in judo

explanation.surface: A single judo champion stands upright on a riverbed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standing up' turns I DAN into NADI, which sits on top of R.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point of anything is its bottom, a synonym for the low point.

clue.text: Wary, adding dodgy fuel to vehicle

indicators.note: adding tells us to attach one piece after the other

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: dodgy means unreliable or not right, so the letters of the word fuel are disordered

explanation.surface: A cautious driver worries about putting suspect fuel into the car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dodgy' looks like it describes bad petrol; here it scrambles the letters of the word fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Being wary means being cautious and taking care, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Catholic priest, perhaps, strangely noticeable? No, no

indicators.note: strangely says the remaining letters are put in an odd order
the second no instructs us to go without the letters of the first

parts.note: the word No supplies the letters to take away

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a Catholic priest stands out oddly, and is firmly told no.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing N and O from NOTICEABLE leaves TICEABLE, which 'strangely' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: Catholic priests take a vow to stay unmarried and abstain from sex, so a priest is an example.

clue.text: Annoying shop assistant providing ointment for example

definitions.meaning: read whimsically, someone irritating who works behind the shop counter
a substance applied to the skin to cause mild irritation that relieves deeper pain, such as a liniment

explanation.surface: A grumpy salesperson hands over a tube of cream.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer into the shop counter and an annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: A liniment that produces surface irritation to distract from deeper pain is a medical example of this remedy.

clue.text: Song about President Lincoln being a lazy sort?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the song's letters go round the president

parts.note: a Lied is a German art song
Abraham Lincoln was known as Abe

explanation.surface: A song about Abraham Lincoln asks whether he was idle.
explanation.walkthrough: A Lied (plural Lieder) is a German art song, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who stays in bed late is a layabout, an idle person.

clue.text: No vegetarian warder

definitions.meaning: read literally, someone who eats beef and so is no vegetarian
a Yeoman Warder at the Tower of London

explanation.surface: A prison guard who is a committed meat-eater.
explanation.walkthrough: Yeoman Warders guarding the Tower of London are popularly called by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The ceremonial guards of the Tower of London are known by this nickname, so one is a warder.

clue.text: Tree visible in the dark, oddly

indicators.note: oddly picks out the letters in the odd-numbered positions

explanation.surface: A tree whose pale bark shows up at night.
explanation.definitionFit: A hardwood from South-East Asia, prized for shipbuilding and furniture, is a kind of tree.

clue.text: Bird served for starters with beef

indicators.note: for starters means taking only the opening letter of the word served

parts.note: with can mean and
to beef is to complain, and so is to grouse

explanation.surface: A game bird is served as a first course alongside beef.
explanation.walkthrough: Both beef and grouse here are verbs meaning complain, not meats.
explanation.definitionFit: These pigeon-like ground birds of dry regions are a family of birds.

clue.text: Test now in the afternoon, presumably

definitions.meaning: an examination of knowledge or skill
if it is afternoon now, it is ex-a.m., formerly morning

explanation.surface: A test is being held now, in the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: In the afternoon it is no longer morning: ex (former) plus a.m.
explanation.definitionFit: An examination of knowledge, as at school, is a test; the second reading is a playful split.

clue.text: Bill probes United Nations graph to no avail

indicators.note: the bill probes the graph, so it pokes inside it

parts.note: a profile is a graph or outline showing variation
a tab is a bill, as in picking up the tab

explanation.surface: A bill pores over a UN chart and gets nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A profile can be a graph or outline showing variation, such as a sales profile.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that earns nothing and is useless is fruitless, done to no purpose.

clue.text: P & O arranged outlandish entertainment

indicators.note: outlandish means bizarre, so the letters are put into a strange order

parts.note: the letters P and O, with the ampersand only joining them

explanation.surface: The ferry company P&O puts on an exotic show.
explanation.walkthrough: P & O is the British ferry and shipping company; only its two letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: A fully sung, serious operatic work on a grand scale is a form of theatrical entertainment.

clue.text: Sri Lankan male bitten by dog

indicators.note: bitten by means the male is held in the dog's jaws, so inside it

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow, or tail, them

explanation.surface: A man in Sri Lanka is bitten by a dog.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dog' is the verb meaning follow, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the people living in northern Sri Lanka and southern India, a nationality example.

clue.text: Press and TV right, intervening in dispute

parts.note: newspapers and television together are the media
a Tory is a right-winger in British politics

explanation.surface: The press and television, leaning right, step into a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: TORY is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party, the political right.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for acting as a go-between to settle a conflict, as an arbitrator does.

clue.text: Flier marking the origin of Communism?

parts.note: communists are called Reds
a start is an origin or beginning

explanation.surface: A leaflet commemorating where Communism began.
explanation.definitionFit: A small songbird with a reddish tail is a bird, and birds are fliers.

clue.text: Film mogul supporting Italian leader? Right

parts.note: pro means in favour of, supporting
Il Duce was the title of Mussolini

explanation.surface: A movie boss is asked whether he backed Mussolini, and agrees.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who finances and oversees making a movie is a typical film boss.

clue.text: Little bird worth less, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word is judged by its sound

parts.note: something worth less is lower in price

explanation.surface: A small bird is apparently of lower value.
explanation.definitionFit: A young bird that chirps, a fledgling chick, is a small bird.

clue.text: Former president snatched by kidnapper once

indicators.note: snatched by means the answer is held inside the following words

explanation.surface: An ex-president was once abducted by a kidnapper.
explanation.definitionFit: Juan Perón was the president of Argentina, a former head of state.

clue.text: Forecast the ruin of Hull?

parts.note: Hull is a port city in Yorkshire, England
an end is a ruin or downfall

explanation.surface: Predicting the downfall of a city or a ship's hull.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull looks like the body of a ship; it is the English port city of Kingston upon Hull.
explanation.definitionFit: To foreshadow or be an omen of something to come is to forecast it.

clue.text: Morning sermon by priest wanting improvement

indicators.note: by means next to, so the pieces are placed side by side

parts.note: Eli is the Biblical priest who taught Samuel
an oration is a formal speech, like a sermon

explanation.surface: A priest giving a morning sermon is looking to better things.
explanation.walkthrough: Eli is the Old Testament priest who raised Samuel, a stock crossword priest.
explanation.definitionFit: Making something better is the act of bettering it, a formal synonym for improvement.

clue.text: Ducks — appropriate to have head lowered

indicators.note: in a down entry the first letter is moved further down the word

parts.note: to appropriate is to steal

explanation.surface: Ducks are told it is fitting to keep their heads low.
explanation.walkthrough: STEAL's head, S, drops to the bottom of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Small freshwater dabbling birds of this name are kinds of duck.

clue.text: Pilot very lost? No way

parts.note: so can mean very, as in so good

indicators.note: No means the way is missing from the word lost

parts.note: ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: A pilot is badly lost and has no route home.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing ST (street) from LOST leaves LO.
explanation.definitionFit: To fly an aircraft alone is to fly unaccompanied, which is piloting by oneself.

clue.text: Mad, reversing over mountain pass

indicators.note: reversing tells us to read the word for a mountain pass backwards

parts.note: a col is a pass between mountains
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A driver goes crazy backing down a mountain pass.
explanation.definitionFit: A slang word, from Spanish, for crazy or insane.

clue.text: One who's on track to arrange the crockery?

parts.note: a plate is a piece of crockery
a layer is one who lays, or arranges, things

explanation.surface: Someone well on the way to setting out the dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on track' means railway track, not making progress.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway worker who lays and maintains the track works on the line, hence on track.

clue.text: Religious text worthily translated

indicators.note: translated means turned into another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sacred book has been rendered faithfully into another language.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred scripture, the Bible regarded as inspired, is a religious text.

clue.text: Detective, mostly insignificant and feeble

parts.note: DI is a Detective Inspector

indicators.note: mostly means dropping the last letter of the synonym

parts.note: small means insignificant

explanation.surface: A detective is described as unimportant and weak.
explanation.definitionFit: A poor, pathetic or weak effort is called pitiful, close to feeble.
